Primates Classification. A persistent misconception distinguishes primates from humans, treating humans as fundamentally separate from the primate order, when in fact Homo sapiens is a species within the order Primates. Primates include lemurs, tarsiers, monkeys, apes, and humans. The confusion arises from the cultural and psychological separation humans maintain from other animals, not from any biological distinction.

Primates is a mammalian order characterized by grasping hands, forward-facing eyes, complex brains, and generally social behavior. Humans fit all of these criteria and are unambiguously classified as primates. The order Primates is divided into two groups: Haplorhini, which are dry-nosed primates including monkeys, apes, and humans, and Strepsirrhini, which are wet-nosed primates including lemurs and lorises. Humans belong to Haplorhini.

Within Haplorhini, humans are members of the family Hominidae, the great apes, alongside orangutans, gorillas, and chimpanzees. This makes humans literally apes in the biological sense. The misconception often stems from education that treats "apes" and "primates" as categories distinct from humans, reinforcing a false separation for cultural and religious reasons.

Genetic evidence shows humans and chimpanzees share approximately ninety-eight to ninety-nine percent of their DNA. Humans and other primates share progressively fewer genetic similarities by evolutionary distance. Modern biological taxonomy, established through evolution and genetics, places humans squarely within Primates. Denying this is akin to denying that humans are mammals.
